newsitem.title: USA: US Treasuries firmer at open, payrolls awaited.
newsitem.headline: US Treasuries firmer at open, payrolls awaited.

text.p: U.S. Treasury prices opened firm on Friday as players awaited the key monthly employment report for January.

The influential report is expected to show that non-farm payrolls expanded by 237,000 jobs in January, according to an average estimate gathered in a Reuters poll. In December, payrolls were reported to have grown by 262,000 jobs.
In early dealings, the 30-year Treasury bond was up 3/32 to 96-25/32, yielding 6.75 percent. Ten-year notes were up 1/32 to 100-9/32, yielding 6.46 percent.
David Sloan, senior economist at I.D.E.A., said that while his own forecast of 235,000 new non-farm payroll jobs is in line with the consensus, "the risks are on the upside on the employment report."
Sloan said seasonal factors make the January payroll number difficult to forecast and that the market would probably move a little lower on the report.
If the non-farm payrolls number turns out to be in line with average expectations, "the market will probably focus on the (average hourly) earnings data," Sloan said.
The market is looking for a two- or three-cent rise in average hourly earnings, said Sloan who, himself, expects a four-cent hourly earnings increase.
A four-cent average hourly earnings gain would create a year-over-year rise of four percent, Sloan noted.
"That would be a negative for the market," he said.
But William Sullivan, senior vice president and director of fixed-income research at Dean Witter Reynolds said the market was poised to do much better if the payroll data do not stand in the way.
"The market has a very upbeat psychology and is prepared to do much better," said Sullivan, citing the "collapse" in gold, weakness in the London oil market and a strong dollar.
"If payrolls show soft or modest growth, we have a channel to do much better today and you could see 6.50 percent or 6.55 percent (30-year bond yield) this month," he said.

Sullivan argued that in January it is difficult to get a "pervasively strong" payrolls report, although there may be pockets of strength. But for the market to go higher, "you do need modest or slow payroll growth," he emphasized.
"If it's a consensus report, the market will probably rally," said Credit Suisse First Boston chief market strategist Matthew Alexy.
Alexy said the market will "think very seriously about what (the payroll data) mean because of seasonal adjustment problems the BLS (Bureau of Labor Statistics) will have.
At the short end of the maturity range, the Treasury three- and six-month bill rates were unchanged at 5.00 percent and 5.07 percent, respectively.
Two-year notes were up 1/32 to 99-31/32, yielding 5.89 percent. Five-year notes were up 3/32 to 100-7/32, yielding 6.20 percent.
